1.pericope_label: Jacob sacrifices at Beersheba and goes down

schools.summary: Calvin weighs what the sacrifice cost a man about to lose the sight of the land that was the type and pledge of the heavenly country, and finds in the renewal of the covenant a remedy against falling from the faith; he also insists that a silent vision would have profited nothing, since superstition snatches at mere spectres and no living image of God can exist without the word. Gill rejects Jarchi's guess that Jacob had signed over everything gained in Padan-aram to Esau for his share in the cave of Machpelah.

Henry remembers the communion Abraham and Isaac had enjoyed at Beersheba, hears in the double call Jacob, Jacob a reminder of his low estate since his present fears scarcely became an Israel, sets out the old man's discouragements one by one, and watches him travel not in a chariot, though his own son rode in one, but in a waggon, for he affected nothing stately.

Clarke answers each of Jacob's fears from the four clauses of the promise — he may go down safely, the covenant will be kept even in Egypt, God will bring his bones back, and Joseph will do him the last kind office; Wesley closes with the arithmetic, sixty-six going down and the house standing at seventy, two hundred and fifteen years after the promise of a great nation, so that the multiplying of those seventy might appear the more illustrious.

Ellicott explains the delay at Beersheba from Jacob's second thoughts — the boding prophecy of bondage, Abraham's charge to Isaac never to leave Canaan, and the command that kept Isaac himself from going down — and reads the closing of the eyes as the office of the nearest in blood; Keil and Delitzsch, with Calvin, point to the painted tomb at Beni-hassan, where strangers arrive in Egypt with their goods on asses and two children in panniers.

debates.question: Was it lawful for Jacob to leave Canaan at all?

sides.position: it might even be a sin, involving the loss of the covenant, since Abraham forbade Isaac to leave and Isaac was himself commanded to stay
the question is settled by the vision, which makes the descent an act of obedience rather than of flight

themes: the sacrifice on the border of the land
fear not to go down into Egypt
I will surely bring thee up again
the waggons and the going down

8.pericope_label: The names of the house of Jacob

schools.summary: Calvin lays the difference between Moses' seventy and Stephen's seventy-five to the transcribers, rejecting the solution that Stephen counted by anticipation three born later in Egypt, and reads the small number as the point of the passage, since the more improbable it looks that seventy should become such a multitude, the more clearly the grace of God shines out of so dry a fountain; he also takes the naming of Shaul's Canaanite mother, alone of all the mothers, for a mark of dishonour on his race. Gill takes the children of Israel here for the body of the people as they stood on the day of the descent, Jacob included.

Clarke relieves the chronology by anticipation, some of the names belonging to persons born during the seventeen years Jacob afterwards spent in Egypt, and prefers Hales's reckoning of Stephen's number, which adds the nine surviving wives to the sixty-six rather than adding names to the text.

Ellicott treats the list as a legal document, the title-deed by which Israel would hold Canaan, drawn up so that grandsons stand as sons and every head of a family counts as born in the land; he then presses the dates hard, finding no space whatever for the sons of Pharez and no room for Benjamin's ten, and remarks that nothing so legitimately produces scepticism as facts marshalled to suit the passage in hand.

debates.question: How is the count of seventy to be squared with the seventy-five of Acts?

sides.position: the Greek number is a transcriber’s error; it crept into one passage only, and a single mark was easily displaced
the Septuagint adds five descendants of Joseph at the naming of his sons, and Stephen followed that text
no addition is needed: the sixty-six omit the sons’ wives, of whom nine were living, and sixty-six with nine is seventy-five

debates.question: Why is Shaul alone given a named mother?

sides.position: to fix a mark of dishonour on his race, the fathers being on guard against mixing with that nation
Jewish tradition made him really Dinah’s son by Shechem, adopted by Simeon to save his sister’s honour

28.pericope_label: Judah sent before, and the meeting in Goshen

schools.summary: Calvin reads Jacob's request as asking no house but only leave to pitch his tent unmolested, uses the weeping to show that the holy Fathers were not destitute of natural affection, defends Joseph against the charge of craft since Pharaoh knew the richness of Goshen and had offered it unasked, and finds the contempt of the Egyptians profitable, since a people loathed is a people not dispersed; Gill takes Judah for the son highest in his father's esteem.

Henry reads the sending of Judah as respect owed to the government under whose protection these strangers came, measures the weeping against the earlier scene with Benjamin, notes how near sorrow and joy stand when the same tears serve for both, and marks the reversal in Joseph's care, that those who once contrived to be rid of him are now settled by him, which is rendering good for evil.

Clarke calls Judah a man of sense and eloquent, reports that the Septuagint knows Goshen as the land of Rameses and identifies it with Heroopolis, and wonders whether old Simeon had this verse in view when he asked to depart in peace; Wesley refuses to read Jacob's now let me die as weariness of life.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the word used for Joseph's showing himself is one generally reserved for the appearance of God, chosen to mark the glory in which he came out to meet his father; Ellicott explains why the family was kept out of the Nile valley, since isolation was indispensable if they were to grow into a nation fit to guard a growing revelation.

debates.question: Who fell on whose neck at the meeting?

sides.position: Jacob fell on Joseph’s neck; Maimonides held that a son would not take so great a liberty with his father, and this gives the most natural sense
Joseph fell on his father’s neck and continued there weeping

themes: why the family was kept separate

schools.summary: Gill explains why the answer had to be exact, since it would direct Pharaoh how to dispose of them, and lists Joseph's further reasons for Goshen — good pasture, nearness to himself, the shortest road back to Canaan, and distance from the heart of the country.

Clarke describes the ground on Bruce's authority as the land never overflowed by the Nile, whose proper name was Geshen, the country of grass, gives three reasons for the Egyptian loathing of shepherds — their reputation as freebooters, the memory of Manetho's king-shepherds, and above all the sacrificing of the very animals Egypt held sacred — and closes with Warburton, that Egypt was the one country where a people so prone to join themselves to the nations could live long and stay unmixed.

Ellicott takes the clause for a remark of the narrator, confirmed by monuments that draw shepherds unshaven and ill-dressed, supposes the Egyptian peasantry left their beasts to women and children, and grounds the dislike in the ordinary hostility of settled men towards wandering clans whose cattle prey on enclosed land.

debates.question: What lay behind the Egyptian abhorrence of shepherds?

sides.position: chiefly that such men sacrificed the ox and the sheep which Egypt worshipped, with the memory of Manetho’s king-shepherds behind it
the Hyksos conquest was possibly later than Joseph; the dislike is the ordinary hostility of a settled people to nomads, with a religious difference on top of it

themes: thy servants have been keepers of cattle
